# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to permanently face its star. This phenomenon, common among close-orbiting exoplanets, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is temperature contrast. The permanent dayside, under constant stellar bombardment, can reach scorching temperatures hot enough to vaporize oceans, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may freeze out entirely. On a tidally locked world without atmospheric heat transport, the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night—might be the only habitable region.

However, atmospheres and oceans dramatically reshape this picture. Winds redistribute heat from dayside to nightside, moderating temperature extremes. Climate models of tidally locked exoplanets suggest that if atmospheric pressure is sufficient, a planet could maintain liquid water across much of its surface. Ocean currents add another transport mechanism, potentially preventing atmospheric collapse on the nightside.

Tidal locking also influences atmospheric composition. Some models predict "eyeball Earths"—worlds where a single eye-like ocean forms beneath the substellar point, surrounded by ice. Others suggest dayside cloud decks form, reflecting starlight and cooling the surface—a self-regulating mechanism that could keep close-orbiting planets temperate.
